strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: jointly selecting intervention and contextual scopes. Its toy SCM clearly illustrates why fixed-scope CoBO and context-free CaBO can be linearly suboptimal.
The proposed decomposition into POMPS arms and contextual BO subproblems is modular and intuitively appealing.
The paper attempts substantial theory, including worst-case and gap-dependent high-probability regret bounds expressed through GP information gain.
Experiments use 110 seeds, confidence intervals, and several noise, context, and GP-backend ablations; the main presentation and figures are generally readable.
weaknesses: The central reduction from general mixed causal policies to contextual GP bandits is not justified. Mixed policies may involve sequential or intervention-dependent contexts, whereas the analysis assumes each arm's context is i.i.d. from a fixed distribution and observed before a joint action. Collapsing scopes having the same unions of intervention and context variables also discards which context controls each action and can change the admissible policy class. Consequently, the stated theory does not establish regret guarantees for the advertised general CoCa-BO setting.

The proof contains consequential errors. In Proposition 1, the inequality f_i^circ(x,c) <= max_c f_i^*(c)-min_c f_i^*(c) is false: the context-optimal value can be constant while action regret is positive. The arm-selection argument also compares post-play statistics that were unavailable when the arm was selected, and Algorithm 2's initialization appears to execute both branches. Thus Theorem 1 is not proved as written.

There is a major theory-implementation gap: the analysis concerns exact GP-UCB with known kernels, independent GP arms, and Gaussian homoscedastic noise, while experiments use HEBO or other learned GP backends and SCMs containing latent, non-Gaussian or heteroscedastic variation. No argument or ablation connects the guarantee to the implemented method.

The evaluation is entirely synthetic and mostly uses examples constructed so that a baseline cannot represent the optimum. Comparisons omit stronger recent causal-BO methods and useful oracle-scope or exhaustive-scope baselines. A decreasing average regret over only 700 rounds is also insufficient evidence for the claimed sublinear asymptotic behavior.

The scalability claim is unsupported. POMPS discovery is acknowledged to be exponential and GP updates cubic, yet no scope-enumeration runtime, memory analysis, or scaling study is reported. The 87-variable example does not explain how its two reported POMPSs were computationally obtained.

Reproducibility is poor despite contrary claims: the manuscript provides no implementation URL or complete kernel, acquisition, beta, rho, and baseline settings. Several SCM specifications are internally inconsistent, including the Cancer/PSA derivation, duplicated U2 notation, and the self-referential equation C4 ~ N(C4,0.1).

Claims such as a general scalable framework, the first CaBO regret bound, consistent convergence to the optimum, and robustness to noise are stronger than the evidence and sometimes conflict with qualifications or cited prior regret results elsewhere in the paper.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem and offers an intuitive unification of contextual and causal Bayesian optimization through mixed policy-scope selection.
The analytical counterexample clearly demonstrates that fixed-scope CoBO and context-free CaBO can incur linear regret.
Combining per-scope contextual BO with bandit-based scope selection is conceptually appealing, and the information-gain analysis is ambitious.
The empirical study uses 110 seeds and includes noise, GP-backend, context-removal, and high-dimensional ablations. The presentation and supplementary material are generally clear.
weaknesses: The proof of the main regret theorem contains a false inequality. In Appendix B.2, the action suboptimality max_x f_i(x,c)-f_i(X_i,c) is bounded by the variation of the context-optimal value, max_c f_i*(c)-min_c f_i*(c). This fails even when f_i is independent of context, invalidating the Azuma-Hoeffding step and therefore Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 as written.

The reduction from general mixed policy scopes to the analyzed multi-function bandit is not justified. Algorithm 2 assumes all contexts are drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution before all joint actions, whereas admissible acyclic mixed policies can contain sequential contexts whose distributions depend on earlier interventions.

Scopes are declared equivalent whenever they have the same unions of intervenable and contextual variables. This discards which context each intervention may depend upon; such scopes can define different feasible policy classes, while the BO routine effectively lets every action depend on every context.

The theoretical algorithm assumes independent, known-kernel GP-UCB models with homoscedastic Gaussian noise, but experiments use learned HEBO models. No guarantee or careful correspondence is established for the implemented method.

Evaluation is limited to hand-designed synthetic SCMs. Scope selection is tested with at most two POMPSs, the high-dimensional example mainly adds explicitly redundant variables, and there are no oracle-scope, alternative bandit-selector, functional/model-based causal BO, or real/semisynthetic comparisons.
Claims of scalability are unsupported by runtime or scaling results despite exponential POMPS enumeration, one GP per scope, and cubic GP updates.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing experimental hyperparameters and no visible code URL despite the public-implementation claim. Appendix SCM specifications also contain errors, including the self-referential C4~N(C4,0.1), and the asserted zero optimum in the PSA example appears incompatible with bounded medication actions and unbounded Gaussian BMI.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem and gives a clear analytical example showing why causal structure and contextual information can both be necessary to avoid linear regret.

The hierarchical design—enumerating possibly optimal scopes, running contextual BO within each scope, and using a bandit rule across scopes—is modular and intuitively useful. The proposed worst-case and instance-dependent information-gain bounds would be meaningful if the technical issues were resolved.
The experiments use 110 seeds with uncertainty bars and include settings where baselines can and cannot attain the optimum, plus noise, backend, context, and dimensionality studies.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with a substantial appendix and clean figures: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-4zu_177c/call-adc44c1bf13e4d1e815c631f7e9bf241/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The reduction from general mixed policy scopes to contextual BO is not justified. An MPS specifies which context each individual intervention may use and can encode sequential decisions, whereas the algorithm collapses scopes having the same unions X(S) and C(S), observes all contexts first, and jointly optimizes all interventions using the full context. This can implement inadmissible policies. The theory additionally assumes a fixed i.i.d. context distribution independent of actions, which does not cover treatment-dependent or intermediate contexts allowed by the stated MPS definition. Thus the convergence result applies to a narrower one-stage problem, not the advertised policy class.

The proof contains a false inequality in the bound on R_T,3: it asserts f_i*(c)-f_i(x,c) is bounded by max_c f_i*(c)-min_c f_i*(c). For a function varying with x but not c, the right-hand side is zero while the left-hand side can be positive. Consequently, the Azuma-Hoeffding increment bound and Theorem 1 are not established as written, even if a repair using an action-domain range may be possible.

The theory and evaluated algorithm are insufficiently connected. The theorem analyzes exact GP-UCB with independent zero-mean GPs, known kernels, homoscedastic Gaussian noise, and convex continuous domains; the experiments use HEBO with learned transformations and also claim support for discrete variables. No guarantee is supplied for that implementation.

The evaluation is entirely synthetic and mostly consists of examples constructed to expose CaBO or CoBO failure modes. It omits several relevant methods discussed in related work, oracle-scope and simple alternative scope-selection baselines, and an ablation of the paper's key running-average UCB selector. This is not enough to support claims of broad superiority or practical utility.

The scalability claim is unconvincing because POMPS enumeration is explicitly exponential and GP updates are cubic, yet no enumeration runtime, end-to-end runtime, memory analysis, or scaling curve is reported. The high-dimensional example mainly adds explicitly redundant variables and therefore does not resolve this concern.

Reproducibility has serious gaps: the PDF provides no code URL or experimental hyperparameters for the crucial beta/rho schedules and BO configuration; Algorithm 2 lacks an else/continue and therefore performs both initialization and a regular selection in the same early iteration; the high-dimensional SCM contains the invalid self-reference C4 ~ N(C4, 0.1); another SCM lists U2 twice; and the paper alternates between reward maximization and PSA minimization without specifying a sign conversion. The empirical quantity based on noisy y_t is also called pseudo-regret despite differing from the theoretical conditional-expectation regret.

weaknesses: The central regret proof contains a false inequality: it bounds the action regret at a context by the variation of the context-wise optimal value across contexts. The latter can be zero while a selected action is arbitrarily suboptimal. Consequently, the stated main theorem is not established as written.

The theoretical reduction does not faithfully cover general mixed causal policies. It assumes each scope has a fixed i.i.d. context distribution independent of interventions and treats scopes with identical unions of action and context variables as equivalent, discarding which context each action may use. This can permit infeasible policies and fails when contexts are downstream of interventions.

There is a substantial theory–implementation gap: the analysis concerns exact GP-UCB with known kernels, Gaussian homoscedastic noise, compact continuous domains, and exact acquisition maximization, whereas experiments use HEBO and other learned/approximate backends, mixed variables, and unbounded Gaussian contexts.

The empirical evaluation is limited to hand-designed synthetic SCMs, several constructed specifically so the chosen CaBO or CoBO baseline cannot attain the optimum. It lacks real or credible semi-synthetic tasks, oracle-scope comparisons, competitive contextual-causal alternatives, and ablations isolating the proposed scope-selection rule.

Claims of scalability are unconvincing because POMPS enumeration is explicitly exponential and GP updates are cubic, yet no enumeration runtime, wall-clock cost, memory scaling, or comparison of computational overhead is reported.

Reproducibility is impaired by missing practical hyperparameters and intervention bounds, an apparent double-action control-flow error in Algorithm 2, and invalid or ambiguous SCM equations such as C4 being sampled conditional on itself and U2 being defined twice. These issues are especially problematic for the purported high-dimensional demonstration.

The paper overstates its conclusions: its 'worst-case' guarantee remains Bayesian and assumption-dependent, the experiments do not establish general sample-complexity reductions, and the claimed general practical framework is much broader than the supported setting.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem and clearly motivates why combining contextual information with causal policy-scope selection can improve over fixed-scope CoBO and context-free CaBO.
The proposed architecture—POMPS reduction, contextual BO within each candidate scope, and bandit-style scope selection—is intuitive and potentially useful for an appropriately restricted setting.
The paper ambitiously develops both worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret bounds using information gain.
The presentation is generally organized and readable, and the experiments use 110 seeds, uncertainty bands, noise tests, backend comparisons, and a context ablation.
weaknesses: The claimed causal framework and the theoretical model do not align in general. The analysis assumes that all context is sampled i.i.d. from a fixed arm-specific distribution before a joint action is selected. A valid mixed policy scope may instead contain sequential decisions where a context is downstream of one intervention and used by another, making its distribution action-dependent. Moreover, collapsing scopes according only to the unions X(S) and C(S) allows every action to depend on every context, potentially producing policies outside the defined policy class. Consequently, the theorem does not establish regret against the general causal policy space claimed in the paper.

A key step in the regret proof is false: the proof bounds the within-context action loss max_x f_i(x,c)-f_i(X,c) by the range of the context-optimal value max_c f_i*(c)-min_c f_i*(c). For a context-independent but action-varying function, the latter is zero while the former can be positive. This invalidates the martingale bound for R_{T,3} and therefore the stated main theorem as written. The arm-count argument also appears to use post-update counts and UCB averages although arm selection uses their pre-update values.

The theory concerns exact GP-UCB with fixed known kernels, independent GP draws across scopes, and additive i.i.d. Gaussian noise. The experiments instead use HEBO with learned transformations and hyperparameters, while several showcased SCMs contain uniform latent confounding and non-Gaussian outcome variation. No argument connects the implemented procedure or examples to the theorem's assumptions.

The empirical evidence is narrow and largely constructed to expose predetermined structural failures of CoBO or CaBO. It consists only of synthetic SCMs, several sharing essentially the same mechanism, and omits competitive scope-selection or causal-BO alternatives, real or established benchmark tasks, sensitivity to graph misspecification, scaling with the number of POMPSs, and runtime comparisons.

The scalability claims are insufficiently supported: POMPS enumeration is explicitly exponential in the number of variables and GP updates are cubic in observations, yet the high-dimensional experiment reports neither enumeration time nor computational scaling and appears to retain only two favorable candidate scopes.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the stated claim of a public implementation: the PDF contains no code link and omits important optimizer and tuning details. The high-dimensional SCM is also invalid as written because it defines C4 recursively as C4 distributed around C4, and another experiment writes U2 twice where U1,U2 is evidently intended.

The novelty and positioning are overstated. In particular, the claim of the first regret bound for the CaBO setting is difficult to reconcile with the paper's own discussion of regret bounds for causal-UCB* and model-based causal BO. Overall, the promising restricted-setting idea does not compensate for the unsupported general causal claims, invalid proof step, and limited evaluation.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a meaningful gap between causal and contextual Bayesian optimisation. Its analytical example clearly motivates why ignoring either causal structure or context can cause linear regret.
The hierarchical combination of POMPS selection with contextual BO is intuitive and could substantially reduce intervention dimensions when the causal graph is known.
The paper targets both worst-case and instance-dependent guarantees and provides extensive derivations and information-gain specialisations.

The empirical protocol uses 110 seeds, confidence intervals, high-dimensional synthetic experiments, and useful noise, context, and GP-backend ablations. The presentation is generally clear. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-mwkfhe0k/call-80fb7adb24b54a25a8cbda8fc072dbee/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central regret proof contains a false inequality. In bounding R_T,3, it asserts f_i^*(c)-f_i(x,c) is at most max_c f_i^*(c)-min_c f_i^*(c). A function independent of context can have zero variation in f_i^* but positive action regret, directly contradicting this claim. Consequently, the martingale-increment bound, Equations (22)-(24), Proposition 1, and Theorem 1 are not established as written.

The reduction from general mixed causal policies to the analysed multi-function BO problem is unsupported. The theory assumes that each arm has a fixed i.i.d. context distribution independent of interventions and homoscedastic Gaussian noise. General compatible mixed scopes can contain contexts affected by earlier interventions, making their distributions policy-dependent; the paper does not state graphical restrictions excluding this case.

Scopes are declared equivalent whenever their aggregate intervenable and contextual sets coincide. This discards the per-intervention assignments C_X that define an MPS. The subsequent BO routine appears to let every intervention depend on every observed context, potentially merging distinct scopes and selecting policies outside the admissible class Π_S.

The experiments use HEBO and other practical backends, whereas the theorem concerns exact GP-UCB with explicit beta and rho schedules. The necessary schedules, kernels, hyperparameters, and correspondence between the implemented and analysed algorithms are not adequately reported.

The evaluation is entirely synthetic and compares mainly against CaBO and CoBO. It omits several related causal-optimisation methods, provides no runtime or scaling study for the exponentially expensive POMPS enumeration and cubic GP updates, and supports the high-dimensional claim with only one hand-designed graph.

Reproducibility is weakened by material pseudocode and SCM inconsistencies: Algorithm 2 lacks an else branch and therefore appears to perform two interactions during each initial round; Appendix A contains repeated-variable and self-referential equations and an apparently missing Cancer term. strengths: The motivation is compelling, and the constructed example clearly illustrates why using either causal structure or contextual information alone can incur linear regret. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-m015cmcm/call-29a0f454614e42548257c01ab823a526/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Combining POMPS selection, contextual BO within each scope, and bandit-style scope selection is conceptually natural and potentially useful.
The paper attempts substantial theory, including worst-case and gap-dependent high-probability regret bounds with information-gain interpretations, and provides detailed appendices.
Experiments use 110 seeds and include noise, GP-backend, context-removal, and deliberately high-dimensional ablations; the presentation is generally clear.
weaknesses: The reduction does not appear valid for general mixed policy scopes. It collapses scopes having the same aggregate intervention and context sets even though different assignments of contexts to individual interventions define different feasible policies. It also selects all actions after observing all aggregate contexts, which can violate the sequential causal ordering permitted by an MPS; in such cases context distributions can depend on preceding interventions rather than being fixed i.i.d. distributions as assumed by the analysis.

A central proof step is false: the proof bounds the within-context action gap max_x f_i(x,c)-f_i(X,c) by the range of the optimal value f_i^*(c) across contexts. A function can have constant f_i^*(c), hence zero contextual range, while having arbitrarily nonzero action gaps. This invalidates the stated Azuma-Hoeffding argument and therefore leaves Theorem 1 unproven as written, even if a repair using action-domain smoothness may be possible.

The theory and implementation are substantially mismatched. The guarantees concern exact GP-UCB with known kernels, independent GP functions across scopes, fixed i.i.d. contexts, and exact acquisition maximization, whereas experiments use HEBO with learned transformations and numerical optimization. Independence across reward functions is also not justified when all scopes arise from one SCM.

The evaluation is confined to synthetic, highly constructed SCMs, several designed specifically so a baseline cannot attain the optimum. Comparisons omit relevant alternatives and diagnostic baselines such as functional/model-based causal BO where applicable, oracle or uniform scope selection, and joint BO over a scope identifier. There is no real or established benchmark.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported: POMPS discovery is acknowledged to be exponential, yet no enumeration runtime or memory results are given, including for the 88-variable example with intentionally redundant variables.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the PDF provides no code link or experimental hyperparameter table, the PSA experiments switch from the maximization formulation to minimization without explaining the sign convention, and Algorithm 2 lacks an else/continue after initialization and therefore appears to select and evaluate twice during each of the first m loop iterations.

The algorithm collapses MPSs whenever their unions of intervention and context variables coincide, discarding which context is allowed to condition which intervention. Joint contextual BO can consequently let every intervention depend on every context, potentially optimizing outside the admissible policy scope or violating causal ordering. No equivalence theorem justifies this relaxation.

The theoretical multi-function abstraction is not convincingly connected to general SCMs: it assumes fixed i.i.d. context distributions, independent GP functions across scopes, and homoscedastic Gaussian noise. These conditions need not hold for scopes induced by the same causal system. Moreover, the experiments use HEBO with learned transformations, whereas the proof analyzes an exact GP-UCB procedure.

The scalability claims are unsupported. POMPS enumeration is explicitly exponential in the graph size and GP updates are stated as O(T^3); the 87-variable experiment gives neither enumeration details nor runtime or memory measurements. The number of arms can itself be exponential.

The empirical evidence is limited to tailored synthetic SCMs and comparisons only with CaBO and CoBO. Relevant causal-BO methods, random or uniform scope selection, an oracle-scope baseline, and an ablation isolating the proposed MAB selector are absent. There is also no systematic dimension or candidate-scope scaling study.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing experimental hyperparameters and a code URL, as well as consequential inconsistencies: Algorithm 2 appears to execute both initialization and regular selection during the first m rounds, one PSA equation omits the Cancer term required by the subsequent derivation, and the high-dimensional SCM contains the self-referential equation C4 distributed around C4.

Claims of a general, scalable framework, diverse evaluation, and the first CaBO regret bound are stronger than the presented evidence and are difficult to reconcile with the paper's own discussion of prior causal-BO regret guarantees. Overall, the promising motivation does not compensate for the unresolved soundness and evaluation issues.

strengths: The manuscript clearly motivates an important setting and gives an instructive analytical example showing why using either causal structure or context alone can be suboptimal. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-hrn4gpkk/call-0c7073856e534e1786f5ba6bce4a7b1e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Combining graphical pruning of policy scopes, contextual BO within each scope, and bandit-style scope selection is intuitive and potentially useful in restricted static-context settings.
The paper attempts both worst-case and instance-dependent regret analysis and relates the bounds to kernel information gain.
The experiments use 110 seeds, report uncertainty, and include noise, BO-backend, and context ablations.
weaknesses: The central reduction does not preserve the stated mixed-policy semantics. The algorithm collapses a scope to the unions X(S) and C(S), jointly chooses every intervention after observing every context, and even treats scopes with different pairings (X,C_X) as equivalent. This can let an intervention depend on variables outside its allowed C_X and cannot represent sequential scopes where a context is downstream of an earlier intervention. In such cases the context distribution is also policy-dependent, contradicting the fixed i.i.d. P_i assumption. Consequently, no valid bridge is established from the analyzed multi-function bandit to optimization over the advertised policy class Π_G.

The main proof contains a false inequality. In the bound on R_T,3, it asserts f_i*(C)-f_i(X,C) <= Δf_i*, where Δf_i* is only the variation of the optimal value f_i*(c) across contexts. The optimal value can be constant across contexts while a selected action has positive, context-dependent suboptimality. This invalidates the stated martingale-increment bound and therefore Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 as proved.

The theorem assumes independent GP functions for different scopes, fixed action-independent context distributions, known kernels, exact UCB maximization, and homoscedastic Gaussian noise. These assumptions are neither derived from a shared SCM nor satisfied by several presented SCMs. Experiments instead use HEBO with learned transformations, so the guarantee does not cover the reported algorithm.

The evaluation is confined to hand-designed synthetic SCMs, usually with only one or two candidate scopes. It omits strong relevant alternatives, oracle-scope and scope-selector ablations, and scaling studies in the number of POMPSs. The high-dimensional example mainly adds graphically identifiable nuisance variables and therefore provides limited evidence of general practical scalability.

The claimed scalable framework still requires exponentially expensive POMPS enumeration and cubic GP updates, yet reports no enumeration time, wall-clock cost, or memory scaling. Parallelizability alone does not substantiate the scalability claim.

Reproducibility is compromised by missing algorithmic settings and several inconsistencies: Algorithm 2 lacks an else/continue after initialization; Appendix A.1.2 omits Cancer from the PSA equation although the next derivation substitutes it; Appendix A.2 repeats U2 instead of defining U1; and Appendix A.3 gives the self-referential equation C4 ~ N(C4,0.1). The manuscript also claims a public implementation without providing a link.

strengths: The paper targets an important gap between causal and contextual Bayesian optimisation and gives clear analytical examples showing why either ingredient alone can incur linear regret.
The proposed combination of POMPS enumeration, per-scope contextual BO, and bandit-based scope selection is intuitive and potentially useful.
Providing both worst-case and instance-dependent regret analyses is ambitious, and the information-gain formulation makes the intended dependence on the number of candidate scopes explicit.
The experiments use 110 seeds with uncertainty estimates and include noise, GP-backend, context, and high-dimensional ablations. The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished.
weaknesses: The algorithm does not faithfully represent the stated mixed-policy class. An MPS specifies a separate context set C_X for each intervention X, but CoCa-BO collapses scopes having the same unions X(S) and C(S), observes the entire union of contexts, and jointly optimizes every action against it. Scopes with identical unions can impose different information constraints and have different optimal values; the algorithm can therefore optimize inadmissible policies. Endogenous or sequential contexts also violate the assumed fixed, policy-independent context distribution. This undermines the claimed guarantee for general POMPSs.

The proof of the principal regret theorem contains a false inequality. On page 27 it bounds the action gap max_x f_i(x,c)-f_i(X,c) by the variation of the context-optimal value, max_c f_i*(c)-min_c f_i*(c). For a context-independent function, the latter is zero while action gaps can be positive. Consequently, the Azuma-Hoeffding bound for R_T,3 and hence Theorem 1 are not established as written. A different bound using variation over the action domain may repair the rate, but that proof is absent.

There is a substantial theory-method mismatch: the theorem analyzes exact GP-UCB with known kernels, Gaussian noise, independent GP functions across scopes, exact acquisition maximization, and fixed i.i.d. context distributions, whereas the experiments use HEBO with learned transformations. The paper does not justify that the independent per-scope GP model is compatible with functions induced by a common SCM.

The evaluation is restricted to hand-constructed synthetic SCMs, several designed so that CaBO or CoBO cannot represent the optimum. It omits relevant alternatives such as Functional Causal BO, model-based causal BO, and causal-UCB, and provides no real-world or established benchmark evidence.

Claims of scalability are insufficiently supported. POMPS enumeration is acknowledged to be exponential and GP updates cubic, yet no enumeration runtime, wall-clock comparison, memory analysis, or scaling study over the number of candidate scopes is reported. The high-dimensional example mainly adds graph-identifiable redundant variables.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the PDF gives no implementation URL or essential optimizer and bandit hyperparameters. Algorithm 2 appears to execute both its initialization branch and the ordinary selection branch in the same round, and experimental SCM specifications contain malformed equations such as C4 being sampled from a distribution centered on itself and U2 being defined twice.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap between causal and contextual Bayesian optimisation, and the proposed decomposition into graph-derived policy scopes, per-scope contextual BO, and bandit-based scope selection is intuitive and potentially useful.
The analytical examples clearly demonstrate why ignoring either context or causal structure can produce linear regret.
The paper attempts substantial theory, including worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret bounds expressed through Gaussian-process information gain.
The experiments use 110 seeds with uncertainty intervals and include noise, BO-backend, context-removal, and high-dimensionality studies.
The manuscript is generally well motivated, clearly organized, and well positioned relative to relevant causal-BO literature.
weaknesses: The central regret proof contains a serious error. It bounds f_i^*(C)-f_i(X,C) by the range of f_i^* over contexts. This is false: the former includes action suboptimality and can be positive even when f_i^* is constant across contexts. Consequently, the Azuma-Hoeffding argument for R_{T,3}, and hence both main regret bounds, are not established.

The arm-count proof also compares indices after the selected arm has been updated, although selection was made using its preceding count. Algorithm 2 additionally lacks an else/continue after initialization, apparently executing two selections during each initial round.

The algorithm collapses mixed policy scopes according only to the unions X(S) and C(S), then optimizes every action jointly as a function of all contexts. This discards the per-intervention restrictions C_X and may produce policies outside the defined class Pi_S, especially for sequential or differently conditioned interventions.

The theory analyzes exact GP-UCB with independent, known zero-mean GP priors and homoscedastic Gaussian noise, whereas experiments use HEBO with learned transformations and incompletely specified exploration parameters. The manuscript does not show that its experimental SCMs satisfy the theoretical model.

The evaluation is restricted to constructed synthetic SCMs tailored to the claimed failure modes. It omits stronger recent causal-BO baselines, an oracle-scope comparison, a direct ablation of the proposed scope-selection rule, real applications, and computational measurements.

Scalability claims are insufficiently supported because POMPS enumeration is explicitly exponential and GP updates are cubic. Reproducibility is further weakened by missing hyperparameter details, no accessible implementation link in the manuscript, and malformed SCM equations such as C4 being defined from itself.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important gap between contextual and causal Bayesian optimisation, with clear analytical examples showing why either source of information alone can incur linear regret. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-wpykxup6/call-9ab2370dc4354cea9f0859b9408dedc5/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
CoCa-BO is conceptually appealing and modular, combining graph-based candidate-scope reduction, contextual BO within each scope, and bandit-based scope selection.

The high-probability worst-case and instance-dependent regret bounds constitute a nontrivial theoretical contribution, and the appendix provides substantial proof detail and information-gain specialisations.
The empirical protocol uses 110 seeds, confidence intervals, explicit SCM equations, and useful ablations covering observation noise, context removal, and alternative GP backends.
The paper is generally well organised and clearly motivates the proposed problem.
weaknesses: The central reduction from mixed causal policies to multi-function contextual BO is not adequately justified. A mixed scope assigns a potentially different context set to each intervention, but the algorithm collapses scopes having the same unions of intervention and context variables and chooses the entire action vector after observing the full context union. In general, this enlarges the feasible policy class beyond the stated scope and can conflate scopes with different optimal values. The regret theorem therefore does not clearly guarantee regret against the original causal-policy class without additional shared, pre-intervention-context assumptions.

The theorem assumes independent GP reward functions across scopes, fixed i.i.d. context distributions, homoscedastic Gaussian noise, and exact GP-UCB optimisation. These conditions are not derived from the SCM formulation and need not hold for general mixed policies, especially when a context is downstream of another intervention. The practical HEBO implementation is also not shown to satisfy the theoretical algorithm's conditions.

The evaluation is entirely synthetic and comprises a small number of heavily constructed SCMs. The high-dimensional example adds many deliberately redundant variables, so it does not convincingly demonstrate robustness on realistic causal systems.

Comparisons are limited to CaBO and CoBO. Relevant alternatives discussed in the paper, oracle-scope variants, random or exhaustive scope-selection baselines, and stronger noncausal BO controls are absent, making it difficult to isolate the benefit of the proposed selection rule.

Scalability claims are insufficiently supported: POMPS enumeration is acknowledged to be exponential and GP updates cubic, yet no preprocessing cost, wall-clock measurements, memory results, or scaling curves are reported. Parallelisability alone does not resolve the worst-case complexity.

Reproducibility is incomplete within the manuscript: it claims a public implementation but provides no accessible link, and practical kernel choices, acquisition and scope-selection hyperparameters, optimisation details, and several variable domains are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and offers an intuitive unification of causal and contextual Bayesian optimisation by treating possibly-optimal mixed policy scopes as arms. The analytical failure example clearly motivates using both causal structure and context. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-89br5lgz/call-2b20c8dd23fa4055920f820ca0555155/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The worst-case and gap-dependent high-probability regret bounds for the resulting multi-function contextual BO problem are potentially valuable and expose dependence on the number of scopes and GP information gain.

The experiments use 110 seeds and confidence intervals, include cases where each baseline can or cannot attain the optimum, and examine noise, GP backend, context removal, and a high-dimensional setting.
The manuscript is generally well organized and supplies extensive definitions, SCM specifications, and proof details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The connection between the causal framework and the analyzed multi-function BO problem is incomplete. The algorithm identifies scopes having the same unions X(S) and C(S), even though different assignments C_X define different feasible policy classes, and then appears to choose every action using all observed contexts. No result shows that this preserves membership in the original mixed-policy scope or its optimum. Likewise, fixed i.i.d. context distributions P_i are assumed without showing that they follow for all admissible mixed policies, particularly when contexts may be downstream of other interventions.

The central regret proof contains a false inequality: on page 27 it bounds max_x f_i(x,c)-f_i(X,c) by max_c f_i^*(c)-min_c f_i^*(c). For a context-independent function with action-dependent reward, the right side is zero while the left side can be positive. This breaks the stated Azuma-Hoeffding argument and leaves Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 unproved as written.

There is a substantial theory-practice gap. The guarantee concerns an exact GP-UCB algorithm with independent GP arms and prescribed beta/rho schedules, while the experiments use HEBO and do not specify how the practical arm-selection bonuses correspond to the analyzed algorithm.

The empirical evidence is restricted to synthetic, hand-designed SCMs and comparisons only with CaBO and CoBO. There are no comparisons with functional/model-based causal BO, causal-UCB-style methods, an oracle-scope BO baseline, or simpler hierarchical bandit alternatives; nor is there a real or established benchmark application.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported: POMPS enumeration is explicitly exponential and the number of arms may itself be exponential. The 86-variable experiment does not report enumeration time, candidate counts, wall-clock cost, or how brute-force enumeration was made feasible, and much of its dimensionality comes from deliberately redundant variables.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The claimed public implementation is not linked, practical hyperparameters are largely absent, Algorithm 2 lacks an else/continue after initialization and thus literally performs two selections in early rounds, and appendix SCM definitions contain errors such as C4 distributed around itself and duplicated U2 in place of U1,U2.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem and gives an effective analytical example showing why causal structure or contextual information alone can produce linear regret.
The proposed combination of POMPS-based scope reduction, contextual BO within each scope, and exploration-aware scope selection is intuitive and potentially useful.
The theoretical ambition is substantial: the paper attempts both worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret bounds using GP information gain.
The experiments use 110 seeds and confidence intervals, include cases where baselines can and cannot attain the optimum, and provide noise, context, and BO-backend ablations.
weaknesses: A key proof step is false: Section B.2 claims that the action regret f_i^*(c)-f_i(x,c) is bounded by the variation of f_i^*(c) across contexts. For example, f(x,c)=-(x-c)^2 has constant f_i^*(c)=0 but positive regret for a suboptimal action. This invalidates the martingale-increment bound used in Proposition 1 and therefore leaves Theorem 1 unproved as written.

The reduction from mixed policy scopes to arms discards essential structure: scopes are declared equivalent using only the unions X(S) and C(S), after which the whole action vector is selected after observing all contexts. Different assignments of context sets C_X to individual intervention variables generally define different admissible policy classes, and no preservation result is given.

The theoretical algorithm uses exact GP-UCB action selection with specified beta and rho schedules, whereas the experiments use HEBO and other backend defaults. The manuscript does not show that these implementations satisfy the theorem or report the practical acquisition functions and schedules, creating a substantial theory–experiment mismatch.

The evaluation is confined to hand-designed synthetic SCMs and compares only against CaBO and CoBO, despite discussing several other causal-optimization methods. The high-dimensional example mostly adds graph-identifiable nuisance variables, so it does not convincingly establish broad practical performance.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported: POMPS discovery is explicitly exponential in the number of variables and GP updates are cubic in observations, yet no enumeration time, end-to-end runtime, candidate-count analysis, or scaling curve is reported.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing experimental hyperparameters and an absent code URL, despite claiming a public implementation. Several SCM specifications also contain consequential errors, including U2 being defined twice and the self-referential equation C4 ~ N(C4,0.1). Algorithm 2 additionally appears to execute both initialization and ordinary selection during each of its first m iterations because it lacks an else/continue branch.

The method assumes a correct known graph, fixed i.i.d. context distributions, and correctly specified independent GP models across scopes; sensitivity to graph misspecification or violations of these assumptions is not evaluated. This is particularly important given the clinical treatment framing.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful gap between causal and contextual Bayesian optimisation. Its constructed example clearly shows that ignoring either causal structure or context can produce linear regret.

CoCa-BO is a conceptually clean combination of possibly-optimal mixed policy scopes, contextual BO within each scope, and bandit-based scope selection. This is a useful and reasonably novel unification of two previously separate settings.

The theoretical contribution is substantial: the paper derives both worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret bounds with explicit dependence on the number of scopes, information gain, and suboptimality gaps, supported by detailed proofs.

The experiments cover complementary success and failure regimes, use 110 seeds, and include a high-dimensional stress test plus ablations for observation noise, GP backend, and contextual information.
The manuscript is generally well organized and provides unusually extensive definitions and appendices.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is entirely synthetic and largely uses SCMs constructed to expose the stated baseline failure modes. Comparisons are limited mainly to CaBO and CoBO; relevant alternatives such as functional/model-based causal BO, generic portfolio methods, and an oracle-scope contextual BO baseline are absent.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported. POMPS enumeration is acknowledged to be exponential in the number of variables, while GP updates are cubic in the number of observations; no runtime, memory, or enumeration-cost results are reported. The specially structured high-dimensional example does not establish general scalability.

There is a significant theory-to-practice gap: the analysis assumes independent, correctly specified GP draws for different scopes, homoscedastic Gaussian noise, fixed i.i.d. context distributions, exact acquisition maximisation, and a known correct graph. Functions induced by different policies in one SCM are generally related, while the experiments use HEBO with learned transformations; the paper does not explain how the theoretical tuning parameters correspond to the implementation.

Collapsing MPSs whenever their aggregate intervention and context sets coincide is not adequately justified. An MPS specifies a separate allowed context set for each intervened variable, whereas the described BO routine appears to choose the entire action vector after seeing the union of contexts. Without an additional constraint or equivalence result, this can admit policies outside the original scope and weaken the connection between the regret theorem and the stated causal-policy problem.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete: no accessible implementation link or full experimental hyperparameter specification is present, Algorithm 2 appears to execute both its initialization block and ordinary selection during the first m iterations, and appendix SCMs contain consequential typographical ambiguities such as U2,U2 and the self-referential C4 distribution.

strengths: Addresses an important intersection of contextual and causal Bayesian optimisation with a conceptually appealing combination of POMPS pruning, contextual BO, and arm selection.
The constructed example clearly demonstrates how ignoring either causal structure or context can produce linear regret.
The paper attempts both worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret guarantees and provides extensive derivations.
Experiments use 110 seeds, confidence intervals, known optima, and useful noise, context, and BO-backend ablations.
The manuscript is generally well organized and positions the method against several relevant causal-optimisation approaches.
weaknesses: The algorithm and theory do not faithfully optimize the mixed policies defined in Section 2. A policy requires each intervention X to depend only on its assigned C_X, whereas Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 optimize the entire action vector after observing the union C(S). Collapsing scopes with identical X(S) and C(S) can therefore merge inequivalent policy classes and permit infeasible dependencies. No equivalence result is proved, so the regret benchmark need not correspond to the stated causal-policy space.

A central proof step is false. In the bound for R_T,3, the paper asserts f_i^circ(x,c) <= Delta f_i^*, where Delta f_i^* is the range across contexts of max_x f_i(x,c). This quantity does not bound variation across actions at a fixed context; with a singleton context it is zero even when action regret is positive. Consequently, Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 are not established as written.

There is a substantial theory-method mismatch: the analysis covers an exact GP-UCB procedure with independent known-kernel GPs, fixed i.i.d. context distributions, and homoskedastic Gaussian noise, while the experiments use HEBO. Several experimental SCMs induce non-Gaussian or action-dependent noise, so they do not validate the theorem's setting.

The evaluation is restricted to a small collection of hand-designed synthetic SCMs, with no real or established benchmark and at most two candidate POMPS arms. Closely related methods discussed in the paper are not evaluated, and there are no oracle-scope, uniform-scope, or alternative arm-selection baselines isolating the proposed selector.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported. POMPS enumeration is explicitly exponential, yet its runtime and memory costs are omitted even for the nominal 86-variable example; parallelizability alone does not resolve this issue.

Reproducibility has concrete gaps: Algorithm 2 lacks an else/continue after initialization and thus appears to perform two interventions per early iteration; the high-dimensional SCM contains the self-referential equation C4 ~ N(C4,0.1); experimental beta/rho and HEBO settings are absent; and the claimed public implementation is not linked in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful gap between contextual and causal Bayesian optimisation. Its analytical example clearly demonstrates why ignoring either context or causal structure can produce linear regret.

The hierarchical idea—restricting attention to graph-derived POMPSs, running contextual BO within each scope, and selecting scopes through an outer bandit—is intuitive and potentially useful for reducing optimisation dimension.
The theoretical development is substantial, attempting both worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret bounds expressed through GP information gain.
The experiments use 110 seeds and confidence intervals, specify several synthetic SCMs, and include noise, backend, context, and high-dimensional ablations.

The manuscript is generally well organised and its figures and algorithms are readable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-86s4gv57/call-c0570082b7d641948e18a350ca6d1b1c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The abstract multi-function model does not cover general mixed policy scopes as claimed. It assumes that the entire context is drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution before a joint action is chosen. A valid MPS can instead be sequential—for example, an early intervention can affect a context used by a later intervention—making the context distribution policy-dependent and preventing the whole action vector from being chosen after observing all contexts. No theorem connects the proposed reduction to such general causal policies.

The equivalence relation in Appendix B.1 discards essential scope structure: two MPSs with the same unions X(S) and C(S), but different assignments C_X to individual intervention variables, generally define different feasible policy classes and can have different optimal values. Treating them as one arm and optimising every action using the full context union may produce an inadmissible policy.

A key proof step for the stochastic-error term is false. On page 27, the proof bounds f_i^*(c)-f_i(x,c) by the range of f_i^* across contexts. For f_i(x,c)=x, for example, the latter range is zero while the former can be positive. This invalidates the Azuma-Hoeffding argument underlying Equations (22)–(24) and therefore leaves Theorem 1 unproved as written. Algorithm 2 also appears to execute both its initialization block and its regular-selection block when t≤m because an else/continue is missing.

The theory and experiments are poorly aligned. The theorem analyzes exact GP-UCB with independent GP functions and homoskedastic Gaussian noise, whereas the main experiments use HEBO and causal response functions sharing one SCM; the flagship SCM also induces non-Gaussian and potentially heteroskedastic residuals. Thus, the experiments do not validate the stated guarantee.

The empirical evidence is too narrow for the broad scalability and superiority claims. All environments are hand-constructed synthetic SCMs, comparator failures are largely built in through infeasible policy scopes, and the high-dimensional example is padded with explicitly redundant variables. Important comparisons such as Functional Causal BO, model-based methods, oracle-scope BO, and simpler scope-selection strategies are absent.

The paper acknowledges exponentially expensive POMPS enumeration but provides no runtime or scaling study, even for the 86-variable example. Hyperparameter and kernel details are insufficient, no code URL is supplied despite the public-implementation claim, and reproducibility is further hindered by apparent SCM errors such as C4∼N(C4,0.1). Sensitivity to causal-graph misspecification is also unexamined.

strengths: The manuscript identifies a meaningful problem—jointly selecting causal intervention scopes and context-dependent policies—and presents the framework clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-b9wpyda1/call-d8a326ed9af44a0facd47a007c5f5cc5/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The analytical example convincingly demonstrates how fixed-scope contextual BO and context-free causal BO can incur linear regret.
The hierarchical combination of POMPS selection with per-scope contextual BO is intuitive and modular, and the attempt to provide both worst-case and gap-dependent regret bounds is valuable.
The empirical study uses 110 seeds, uncertainty bars, noise tests, backend comparisons, and a context ablation; the paper and appendix are generally readable.
weaknesses: The theoretical reduction does not justify the paper's general causal claims. It assumes that each arm has a fixed i.i.d. context distribution and that all contexts are observed before the complete intervention vector is selected. General mixed policy scopes allow contexts downstream of other interventions, so their distributions can depend on the policy and interventions may require sequential ordering. Collapsing scopes having the same unions of intervention and context variables also discards which context conditions which intervention.

There is a concrete gap in the main proof. In Proposition 1, the action regret f_i^*(C)-f_i(X,C) is bounded by the range of f_i^*(C) over contexts. This inequality is false in general: the contextual optimum can be constant while a selected action is substantially suboptimal. Consequently, the Azuma bound for R_{T,3}, and hence Theorem 1 as written, is not established.

The theory analyzes exact GP-UCB with known kernels, independent GP arms, and homoscedastic Gaussian noise, whereas experiments use HEBO with learned transformations and synthetic SCMs whose residual randomness is often non-Gaussian. The manuscript does not establish that the implemented algorithm satisfies the theorem's assumptions or tuning requirements.

The evaluation is limited to bespoke synthetic SCMs. Most comparisons deliberately place CaBO or CoBO outside the policy class needed to attain the optimum, and there are no competitive mixed-policy baselines, oracle-scope controls, or real/semi-synthetic applications. Thus the experiments provide weak evidence beyond representational advantage.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported: POMPS enumeration is acknowledged to be exponential, the number of arms can itself be exponential, and GP updates are cubic in observations. Parallelizability and one specially structured high-dimensional example do not resolve these bottlenecks; no runtime or memory scaling is reported.

Reproducibility has notable omissions and inconsistencies, including unspecified practical UCB/MAB and HEBO settings, no resolvable code URL in the PDF, an apparent cyclic equation C4 ~ N(C4,0.1) in the large SCM, a missing else/continue in Algorithm 2, and an unexplained switch from reward maximization to PSA minimization.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important gap between causal and contextual Bayesian optimisation, and the constructed example in Figure 1 clearly illustrates why either source of information alone can produce linear regret. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-_3_7u04o/call-a904e88d16c84896ac4859cda6b94c68/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The proposed combination of POMPS-based scope reduction, per-scope contextual BO, and bandit-style scope selection is intuitive and modular.

The paper attempts substantial theoretical support, including worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret bounds with explicit dependence on the number of scopes and GP information gain.
The experiments use 110 seeds and confidence intervals, and include useful studies of noise, GP backend, contextual information, and a high-dimensional redundant-variable setting.
The exposition and visual presentation are generally well organized, with helpful notation tables, analytical optima, and detailed appendices.
weaknesses: The proof of the central regret theorem contains a serious invalid step. On page 27, it asserts that the action suboptimality f_i*(c)-f_i(x,c) is bounded by max_c f_i*(c)-min_c f_i*(c). This is false: the contextual optimum can be constant across contexts while a selected action remains arbitrarily suboptimal. This bound is used to control the martingale increments and hence R_T,3, so Theorem 1 is not established as written.

The connection between the theorem and the stated causal problem is incomplete. The analysis assumes each scope has a fixed i.i.d. context distribution P_i and an independent reward function f_i. In a general mixed-policy SCM, interventions can alter the distribution of contextual descendants. The paper does not prove that its POMPS setting satisfies the multi-function BO assumptions.

The method declares two MPSs equivalent whenever their aggregate intervention and context sets coincide, ignoring which context C_X is permitted for each intervention X. These scopes need not have the same admissible policies. Optimising the entire intervention vector after observing the union of contexts can implement a policy outside either original MPS or violate its causal ordering.

Algorithm 2 is internally ambiguous: during the first m iterations, the initialization branch is followed by the ordinary selection block because there is no else or continue, apparently producing two plays per iteration. Moreover, the theorem analyses exact GP-UCB action selection, whereas the experiments use HEBO; the implemented scope index and choices of beta and rho are insufficiently specified.

The empirical comparison is narrow. Only CaBO and a particular full-scope CoBO baseline are evaluated, despite discussion of Functional Causal BO, Model-Based Causal BO, causal-UCB, and related methods. There is also no ablation against simpler hierarchical contextual-bandit scope selectors.

All evaluations use hand-designed synthetic SCMs with known exact graphs and analytic optima. The PSA example is still synthetic, and the high-dimensional experiment largely adds known redundant variables. There is no realistic application, graph-misspecification study, or evaluation under broader noise/model misspecification.

Claims of scalability and practicality are not convincingly supported: POMPS enumeration is exponential in the number of variables, GP updates are stated as cubic in observations, and no enumeration time, wall-clock cost, memory use, or scaling curve is reported.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the claimed public implementation. The PDF supplies no code URL or artifact identifier and omits important hyperparameters. Several SCM definitions also contain consequential apparent errors, including “U2,U2” instead of “U1,U2” and the self-referential equation C4 ~ N(C4,0.1), which is not a valid acyclic SCM.

The paper repeatedly characterizes its assumptions and conclusions as general or mild, but relies on a correct known causal graph, known kernels, independent GP priors across scopes, compact convex domains, and homoscedastic Gaussian noise. These restrictions—and the gap between them and the HEBO experiments—are not adequately acknowledged.

strengths: The paper targets an important gap between causal and contextual Bayesian optimisation and gives a concrete SCM where ignoring either context or causal structure provably incurs linear regret. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-uqjs_nrj/call-306969e67c4c4283b86ee9652eb10478/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The proposed architecture—POMPS restriction, contextual BO within each scope, and bandit-based scope selection—is intuitive and modular.
The multi-function GP-UCB analysis is substantial: it provides both worst-case and gap-dependent high-probability regret bounds expressed through information gain.
The experiments use 110 seeds and confidence intervals, include cases where both baselines can and cannot attain the optimum, and add noise, BO-backend, context, and high-dimensional studies.
The main exposition is generally clear, and the appendix supplies detailed theorem proofs and explicit synthetic SCMs.
weaknesses: The central causal guarantee is not established for the stated framework. A general mixed policy scope has variable-specific contexts and may be sequential, with an upstream intervention affecting a context used by a later intervention. The analysis instead collapses scopes using only the unions X(S) and C(S), samples the entire context i.i.d. from a fixed distribution before choosing all actions, and permits an arbitrary joint action function of that union. This can introduce dependencies not allowed by the original scope and cannot represent intervention-dependent contexts. No reduction theorem bridges the general SCM problem and this narrower static contextual-bandit model.

There is a substantial theory–practice gap. The theorem assumes independent, exactly specified zero-mean GPs across scopes, fixed i.i.d. contexts, homoscedastic Gaussian noise, exact UCB maximisation, and prescribed beta/rho schedules. Response functions induced by one SCM are generally coupled, while the experiments use HEBO and latent-variable SCM noise without showing that these assumptions or the theoretical algorithm apply.

The claimed scalability is unconvincing: POMPS enumeration is explicitly exponential, one GP is maintained per scope, every scope must be sampled, and GP updates are cubic. The high-dimensional experiment has only two candidate scopes and reports neither enumeration time nor performance as the number of POMPSs grows.

The empirical evidence is limited to constructed synthetic SCMs. Comparisons omit recent methods discussed in the paper, an oracle-scope baseline, simple scope-selection alternatives, and real or credible semi-synthetic tasks. Consequently, the broad claims of consistent superiority and practical sample-complexity reduction are insufficiently supported.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no accessible code location, kernel/acquisition settings, beta/rho values, baseline tuning protocol, or runtime results are provided. Algorithm 2 appears to execute both its initialisation and regular-selection blocks during the first m rounds, and Appendix A.3 contains an invalid self-referential equation C4 ~ N(C4,0.1), alongside other notation errors.

Novelty and positioning need strengthening. The method largely composes existing POMPS enumeration, contextual BO, and arm-level UCB, while related bandit/model-selection work is not adequately discussed; moreover, the claim of the first CaBO regret bound is difficult to reconcile with regret results for causal-UCB and model-based causal BO cited by the paper itself.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap between contextual and causal Bayesian optimisation. Its constructed example clearly shows why ignoring either context or causal structure can cause linear regret. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xmos9709/call-b947da8c147b4358aefc7758cd026186/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The combination of possibly optimal mixed policy scopes, per-scope contextual BO, and bandit-based scope selection is intuitive and potentially useful.
The theoretical component is ambitious, offering both worst-case and gap-dependent high-probability bounds with explicit information-gain dependence.
The experiments use 110 seeds and include noise, GP-backend, context-removal, and high-dimensional stress tests; the presentation and figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The algorithm does not faithfully implement the stated mixed-policy class. Definition 2 restricts each intervention X to its assigned context set C_X, but the optimiser operates jointly on X(S) and the union C(S), and Section B treats scopes with equal unions as equivalent. This can let every intervention depend on every context, even when that policy is inadmissible or introduces a causal cycle. Different context-to-intervention pairings with identical unions need not have the same optimum.

A crucial proof step is false in general. The bound f_i^o(x,c) <= Delta f_i^*, used to control martingale increments in Section B, compares action suboptimality with the variation of the context-wise optimum. For f(x,c)=-(x-c)^2, for example, f^*(c)=0 has zero variation while suboptimal actions have positive loss. Consequently, the Azuma-Hoeffding argument and both stated regret bounds are not established as written.

The connection between the causal problem and the theoretical multi-function model is insufficiently justified. The analysis assumes fixed i.i.d. context distributions and independent GP functions across scopes, whereas contexts in a general compatible mixed scope may be affected by interventions and scope-specific response functions arise from the same SCM. The synthetic experiments also use latent, generally non-Gaussian noise and HEBO with learned transformations, so they do not instantiate the analyzed model.

The empirical evidence is too narrow for the paper's broad claims: all environments are synthetic variants of a small number of constructed SCMs. Comparisons omit relevant functional/model-based causal BO methods, causal-UCB-style approaches, an oracle-scope baseline, and an ablation isolating the proposed scope-selection index. The high-dimensional experiment largely adds known-irrelevant variables and does not test end-to-end POMPS enumeration.

Scalability and reproducibility remain weak. POMPS discovery is explicitly exponential and GP updating cubic, yet no enumeration time, wall-clock cost, memory use, or scaling curve is reported. The claimed public implementation is not linked, key optimizer and bandit parameters are absent, Algorithm 2 appears to execute both initialization and ordinary selection during each of its first m iterations, and some supplied SCM equations are self-referential or mistyped. These problems make the current submission insufficiently sound and verifiable for acceptance despite its promising idea.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful gap between contextual and causal Bayesian optimisation. Its counterexample clearly demonstrates why either causal structure or contextual information alone can be insufficient.
The hierarchical combination of POMPS selection and within-scope Bayesian optimisation is intuitive and potentially useful for reducing intervention-search dimensionality.

Under the abstract multi-function GP-bandit model, the paper provides detailed worst-case and gap-dependent high-probability regret analyses with explicit dependence on the number of scopes and information gain.
The experiments use 110 seeds and include high-dimensional, noise, GP-backend, and context ablations.
weaknesses: The central reduction is not valid for general mixed policy scopes. The method collapses each scope to the unions X(S) and C(S), treats scopes with identical unions as equivalent, and optimises an arbitrary joint mapping x(C(S)). This ignores the required per-variable restrictions pi_{X|C_X}. Its fixed i.i.d. context model also excludes valid sequential scopes in which a context depends on an earlier intervention. Consequently, the algorithm may optimise policies outside the stated policy class, and the theorem does not establish regret for the general CoCa-BO problem.

There is a substantial theory–practice mismatch. The proof covers exact GP-UCB with independent zero-mean GPs, known kernels, fixed context distributions, homoscedastic Gaussian noise, exact acquisition maximisation, and prescribed beta/rho schedules. The experiments instead use HEBO or other practical backends, while several SCM-induced reward processes are dependent across scopes and have non-Gaussian or heteroscedastic residuals. No result or diagnostic bridges this gap.

The evaluation is limited to specially constructed synthetic SCMs and compares only against CaBO and CoBO. It omits relevant functional/model-based causal methods, causal-UCB variants, random or standard BO baselines, and an oracle-scope baseline. The high-dimensional experiment mainly adds 77 deliberately redundant variables and provides no runtime or broader scalability evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code location is supplied despite the public-implementation claim, and essential kernel, acquisition, beta/rho, domain, and optimiser settings are absent. Several SCM descriptions are internally inconsistent: Appendix A.1.2 uses Cancer in a derivation although it is omitted from the PSA equation, Appendix A.3 defines C4 from itself, Appendix A.2 duplicates U2, and Appendix A.4 ignores the displayed 0.1 coefficients when computing variance.

The claimed scalability is unsubstantiated. POMPS enumeration is acknowledged to be exponential in the number of variables and GP updates cubic in the horizon, yet enumeration times, optimisation costs, and memory use are not reported; parallelisability alone does not resolve this limitation.

Algorithm 2 is malformed as written: after the initialization branch for the first m rounds, it executes the ordinary selection branch in the same iteration because there is no else/continue, resulting in two pulls and potentially invalid counters. Claims such as being the first CaBO regret bound and consistently reaching the optimum are also broader than the cited theory and experiments support.

strengths: Addresses an important problem by combining contextual and causal Bayesian optimisation and selecting among graph-derived mixed policy scopes.
The analytical example clearly demonstrates why ignoring either context or causal structure can incur linear regret.
The hierarchical POMPS-selection plus contextual-BO design is intuitive, and the paper attempts both worst-case and instance-dependent regret analysis.
Experiments use 110 seeds with uncertainty estimates and include noise, backend, context, and high-dimensional ablations.
weaknesses: The central regret proof is invalid as written. In bounding the martingale term, it asserts f_i^*(c)-f_i(x,c) is bounded by max_c f_i^*(c)-min_c f_i^*(c). This is false—for example, when f varies with x but not c—and therefore the Azuma bound and Theorem 1 do not follow. A repair using the action-domain range may be possible, but is not provided.

The algorithm merges POMPSs having the same unions of intervention and context variables, ignoring which context is allowed to condition each intervention. Optimising a joint action over the full context union can produce policies outside the original mixed policy scope, so the algorithm is not clearly aligned with the stated causal policy class.

The evaluated HEBO-based implementation differs materially from the exact GP-UCB procedure covered by the theorem; learned transformations, approximate acquisition optimisation, and practical exploration parameters receive no guarantee.

Evaluation is limited to hand-designed synthetic SCMs tailored to illustrate the proposed failure modes. Comparisons omit several related causal-BO methods, an oracle-scope baseline, runtime/scaling measurements, and realistic tasks.

Claims of scalability are inadequately supported: POMPS enumeration is exponential, one GP is maintained per candidate scope, and updates are described as cubic in observations. Parallelisability does not resolve worst-case scaling.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing implementation links and important specification errors: the Appendix A.1.2 derivation requires a Cancer term absent from the printed PSA equation, Appendix A.3 defines C4 recursively from itself, and the reported noise variance ignores the stated 0.1 coefficients.

Algorithm 2 appears to execute both its initialization block and its regular arm-selection block during each of the first m iterations because it lacks an else/continue, contradicting the analysis that initially plays each arm once.

The theory relies on known causal structure, independent per-scope Gaussian processes, known kernels, i.i.d. contexts, and homoscedastic Gaussian noise; the manuscript does not convincingly connect these assumptions to the shared-SCM setting or the experimental implementation.

strengths: The paper motivates an important problem and gives clear examples showing why combining causal structure with contextual decision-making can outperform fixed-scope CaBO or CoBO.
The modular combination of POMPS enumeration, per-scope Bayesian optimisation, and bandit-based scope selection is intuitive and could be useful under a suitably restricted setting.
The presentation is generally organized, and the empirical study uses 110 seeds, confidence intervals, noise tests, and GP-backend ablations.
weaknesses: The reduction from mixed policy scopes to ordinary contextual-BO arms is not valid in general. The algorithm collapses scopes having the same unions X(S) and C(S), discarding which context C_X is available to each intervention. It then chooses every action using all contexts, thereby optimizing a generally larger, potentially non-implementable policy class. Moreover, contexts permitted by the MPS definition can be downstream of earlier interventions, whereas the analysis assumes they are drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution before a joint action is chosen.

The central regret proof contains a false inequality. On page 27, the action gap f_i^*(c)-f_i(x,c) is bounded by the variation of f_i^*(c) across contexts. For a context-invariant function, that variation is zero although suboptimal actions can have positive gap. This invalidates the martingale-increment bound and consequently the stated high-probability regret theorem. The arm-selection proof also appears to compare post-update indices even though selection uses pre-update counts.

The theory does not cover the evaluated implementation: it analyzes exact GP-UCB with known kernels, independent GP draws across scopes, fixed context distributions, and homoscedastic Gaussian noise, while experiments use learned HEBO/BoTorch/GPflow routines and SCMs whose scope responses are dependent and can have non-Gaussian or heteroscedastic residuals.

The evaluation is restricted to tailored synthetic SCMs. Several comparisons make a baseline structurally incapable of attaining the optimum, the core scope selector is exercised with only one or two candidate scopes, and the high-dimensional experiment primarily pads the model with redundant variables. Missing comparisons include Functional Causal BO, Model-Based Causal BO, causal-UCB variants, oracle-scope methods, and simple hierarchical-bandit alternatives.

The claimed scalability is unsupported: POMPS discovery is explicitly exponential and GP updates are cubic in the horizon, yet enumeration time, optimization runtime, and memory are not reported—even for the 86-variable example.

Reproducibility is compromised by consequential specification errors: Algorithm 2 lacks an else/continue after initialization and would perform a second update with undefined counts; Appendix A.1.2 omits the Cancer term required by its subsequent algebra; Appendix A.2 duplicates U2 instead of defining U1; and Appendix A.3 specifies the self-referential equation C4 ~ N(C4, 0.1). No implementation URL or sufficient hyperparameter details are provided.

strengths: The paper tackles an important gap between contextual and causal Bayesian optimization by jointly selecting mixed policy scopes and context-dependent interventions. The framing is intuitive and potentially useful.
The analytical counterexamples clearly illustrate why using only causal structure or only contextual information can incur linear regret.
The multi-function BO formulation and attempt to provide both worst-case and gap-dependent high-probability regret bounds are substantial theoretical contributions.
The experiments use 110 seeds and include high-dimensional, noise, GP-backend, and context ablations. The manuscript is generally well organized and provides extensive supplementary derivations.
weaknesses: The main regret proof contains a concrete invalid step. In bounding R_T,3, it claims max_x f_i(x,c)-f_i(X,c) is bounded by max_c f_i^*(c)-min_c f_i^*(c). This is false: for f(x,c)=x independent of c, the latter is zero while action regret can be positive. Consequently, Theorem 1 is not established as written, although a different action-domain range bound might repair the argument.

The reduction from general mixed policy scopes to multi-function contextual BO is insufficiently justified. It collapses scopes with the same unions X(S) and C(S), ignoring which contexts each action may use, and then chooses every action after observing the full context union. For scopes with different per-action information or sequential dependencies, this can optimize an enlarged or causally infeasible policy class. The fixed-i.i.d.-context assumption also excludes scopes whose context distribution depends on an earlier intervention.

The practical method uses HEBO with learned transformations and hyperparameters, whereas the guarantee concerns an idealized GP-UCB procedure with known kernels and prescribed beta/rho schedules. No evidence connects the implemented algorithm to the theorem.

The evaluation is entirely synthetic and omits important recent or oracle comparisons, including Functional Causal BO, model-based causal BO, causal-UCB-style methods, and an oracle-scope version. The high-dimensional comparison largely contrasts an oracle graph-reduced search space against an intentionally 86-dimensional CoBO space.

Scalability is not convincingly demonstrated: POMPS enumeration is acknowledged to be exponential, every scope maintains a separate GP, and GP updates are cubic, yet scope-enumeration runtimes and scaling with the number of candidate scopes are not reported.

Reproducibility has notable gaps: essential optimizer, kernel, acquisition, and exploration settings are absent; no implementation URL appears in the manuscript; Algorithm 2 lacks an else/continue after initialization; and several SCM equations contain apparent inconsistencies or self-references. The maximization regret definition is also not reconciled with the PSA minimization experiments.
