strengths: The manuscript addresses an important and underexplored problem: jointly selecting causal intervention scopes and context-dependent policies. The examples clearly demonstrate why causal-only and context-only optimization can incur linear regret. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-_uynk8lh/call-809fca831af24b1982dbcbc10c6f0d35/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The proposed combination of POMPS-based causal pruning, contextual Bayesian optimization, and bandit-based scope selection is intuitive, modular, and potentially useful.
The worst-case and instance-dependent regret objectives are ambitious, and the analysis explicitly connects regret to the number of candidate scopes, suboptimality gaps, and GP information gain.
The experiments use 110 seeds and include targeted comparisons, a high-dimensional synthetic setting, noise tests, context ablation, and multiple BO backends.
The paper is generally well organized, and the appendix provides substantial mathematical and experimental detail.
weaknesses: The main regret theorem is not established by the supplied proof. In the bound on the martingale term, the paper asserts that the within-context action gap max_x f_i(x,c)-f_i(X,c) is bounded by the range of the context-optimal value f_i*(c) across contexts. This is false: for f(x,c)=x, f*(c) is constant while the action gap can be positive. This invalidates Proposition 1 and hence Theorem 1 as written, even if a revised argument using an action-domain Lipschitz bound may be possible. The arm-count proof also appears to use post-update counts in an index comparison made before the selected arm is updated.

The reduction from general mixed causal policies to the analyzed multi-function contextual bandit is insufficiently justified. The theory assumes a fixed i.i.d. context distribution for each scope and chooses the entire intervention vector after observing the union of its contexts. General mixed policy scopes can have action-specific context sets and sequential causal ordering; collapsing scopes that share only X(S) and C(S) can permit dependencies not allowed by either original scope. Thus, the guarantees do not clearly apply to the causal problem initially defined.

There is a substantial theory-method mismatch: the theorem concerns exact GP-UCB optimization with prescribed confidence sequences and independent known GP priors, whereas the experiments primarily use HEBO and heuristic acquisition optimization. No evidence is given that the implemented procedure satisfies the theorem's conditions.

The evaluation consists almost entirely of closely related, hand-designed synthetic SCMs. Comparisons are limited mainly to CaBO and a fixed-scope CoBO baseline, with no empirical comparison to functional/model-based causal BO, causal-UCB variants, generic hierarchical BO, or oracle scope-selection baselines. This is insufficient for broad claims of consistent superiority across diverse environments.

The scalability claim is not convincingly supported. POMPS enumeration is acknowledged to be exponential and GP updates cubic in the number of observations, yet no enumeration runtime, end-to-end runtime, memory analysis, or scaling curve is reported. A single 86-variable construction run using up to 120 CPUs does not resolve this concern.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the PDF claims a public implementation but provides no code URL, and omits important kernel, acquisition-optimization, confidence-parameter, and baseline-tuning details. The appendix also contains invalid or ambiguous SCM specifications, including duplicated U2 where U1,U2 are needed and the self-referential equation C4~N(C4,0.1), as well as an unexplained maximization/minimization sign mismatch in the PSA experiments.

strengths: The manuscript tackles an important problem by combining causal scope selection with context-conditioned interventions; the motivating counterexample clearly shows how fixed-scope CoBO and context-free CaBO can suffer linear regret. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-i41rawzz/call-f103d88cc98f4837be8a27a8728e879c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Using POMPSs as arms is a conceptually appealing, modular way to exploit a known causal graph while avoiding optimization over every possible policy scope.
The work ambitiously develops both worst-case and gap-dependent regret analyses and connects them to standard maximum-information-gain results for several kernels.
The empirical study uses 110 seeds, confidence bands, multiple constructed failure modes, a high-dimensional example, noise tests, and an ablation across three BO backends.
weaknesses: A key step in the central proof is false. Appendix B bounds f_i^circ(X,C) by Delta f_i^*, where Delta f_i^* is the range of the context-optimal value f_i^*(c). A context-independent function can have Delta f_i^*=0 while a suboptimal action has positive regret. This invalidates the stated martingale-difference bound and consequently Equations (22)-(24), Proposition 1, and Theorem 1 as currently proved.

The instance-dependent theorem uses the arm-averaged information gain bar-gamma in its leading term, whereas Equation (21) and the final proof calculation use c(T), defined with the generally larger gamma(T). No argument justifies replacing gamma(T) by bar-gamma(T), so the advertised bound and scaling are unsupported.

Algorithm 2 is internally inconsistent: its initialization branch lacks an else/continue and therefore appears to perform two selections and observations in each of the first m iterations. Moreover, Lemma 4 compares indices at post-pull counts even though selection occurs using pre-pull counts. These issues further weaken confidence in the proof-algorithm correspondence.

The theory does not cover the evaluated implementation. It analyzes independent, known-kernel GP-UCB models with exact UCB maximization, while experiments use HEBO with learned transformations and an insufficiently specified scope-selection update. Response surfaces from different scopes of one SCM are also generally related rather than independent.

The evidence is restricted to hand-designed synthetic SCMs and omits several relevant methods discussed in the related-work section, as well as oracle-scope and scope-selector ablations. Thus the broad superiority and practical-utility claims are not convincingly established.

The scalability claim conflicts with the admitted exponential-time brute-force POMPS enumeration and cubic GP updates; no enumeration counts, preprocessing runtimes, or scaling measurements are reported, even for the claimed 86-variable experiment.

Reproducibility is compromised by missing hyperparameters and no identifiable code link, along with malformed experimental definitions: Appendix A.1.2 omits the Cancer term that is subsequently substituted into PSA, Appendix A.3 specifies the self-referential equation C4 distributed around C4, and Appendix A.4's variance calculation ignores the 0.1 coefficients in the stated SCM.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for a top-tier AI conference with an acceptance rate of about 30%.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score according to the rating scale below.
Choose an OA score from: 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, or 10.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
A paper with fundamental problems such as well-known or trivial results, serious technical flaws, unsupported central claims, invalid evaluation, or unaddressed ethical concerns.

3 = Reject
A paper that is not competitive for a top-tier AI conference due to meaningful weaknesses in novelty, technical soundness, evaluation, reproducibility, clarity, significance, or positioning.
A paper can receive 3 even if it is understandable, technically plausible, or has some strengths, if the overall contribution or evidence is insufficient.

5 = Marginally below the acceptance threshold
A technically solid paper with some positive qualities, but where the reasons for a lower score slightly outweigh the reasons for a higher score.
Typical reasons include limited novelty, incomplete evaluation, weak or missing baselines, insufficient ablations, unclear significance, narrow scope, limited reproducibility, or claims that are stronger than the evidence.
Please use sparingly.

6 = Marginally above the acceptance threshold
A technically solid paper where the reasons for a higher score clearly outweigh the weaknesses.
A rating of 6 requires concrete positive evidence that the paper is competitive for a top-tier AI conference, such as a clear contribution, convincing evaluation, appropriate baselines, and sufficient support for the main claims.
Do not assign 6 merely because the paper is coherent, plausible, or has some positive results.
Please use sparingly.

8 = Accept
A strong paper with a clear and meaningful contribution, convincing technical quality, good-to-excellent evaluation, appropriate comparisons, sufficient reproducibility, and clear relevance to the field.
The paper should have high impact on at least one sub-area of AI or moderate-to-high impact on more than one area of AI.
Minor weaknesses are acceptable, but there should be no major unresolved issues in soundness, evaluation, novelty, or ethics.

10 = Strong Accept
An exceptional paper with groundbreaking impact on one or more areas of AI, technically excellent work, exceptionally strong evaluation, strong reproducibility and resources, and no unaddressed ethical considerations.
This rating should be reserved for rare submissions that are clearly among the best papers in the venue.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

strengths: The paper gives a clear and meaningful unification of contextual and causal Bayesian optimisation. Its analytical SCM example convincingly demonstrates that context-only and causal-only approaches can each suffer linear regret while an appropriate mixed policy is optimal. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-a0t2sgua/call-0dc8f13a4b654c68ae54a70e6e7008e7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The hierarchical construction—restricting attention to possibly optimal mixed policy scopes, selecting among them as bandit arms, and running contextual BO within each scope—is principled and practically interpretable.

The worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret bounds are substantial contributions. The information-gain analysis also makes the dependence on the number of scopes, kernels, and suboptimality gaps informative.

The experiments use 110 seeds, confidence intervals, cases where baselines can and cannot attain the optimum, a constructed high-dimensional environment, and useful noise, context, and GP-backend ablations.
The manuscript is generally well organised and provides algorithms, SCM equations, proofs, and experimental details in an extensive appendix.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is entirely synthetic and largely designed around the proposed method's motivating failure cases. Comparisons are limited mainly to CaBO and CoBO; direct evaluation against Functional CBO, model-based causal BO, causal-UCB-style methods, or alternative scope-selection strategies is absent.

The claimed scalability is not convincingly established. POMPS enumeration is explicitly exponential and GP updates are cubic, yet there is no runtime, memory, candidate-scope, or graph-size scaling study. The high-dimensional example mainly adds deliberately redundant variables and does not resolve the enumeration bottleneck.

The theoretical causal connection requires stronger qualification. The analysis assumes fixed i.i.d. context distributions, independent GP functions across scopes, and additive Gaussian noise. General mixed policy scopes may instead contain sequential or intervention-dependent contexts, and the paper does not formally show that the original SCM problem reduces to the analysed multi-function BO setting.

Collapsing scopes whenever they have the same unions of intervened and contextual variables appears to discard which context variables each intervention is permitted to use. A joint contextual BO over those unions may therefore optimise a larger, potentially causally incompatible policy class unless an additional equivalence result is proved.

There is a concrete proof gap: the Proposition 1 argument bounds action regret at a fixed context by the range of the context-optimal value across contexts, which is not generally valid. A bound using smoothness and the action-domain diameter may repair the argument, but the stated proof is incomplete. Algorithm 2 also appears to perform both initialization and regular selection when t≤m because it lacks an else or continue.

The experiments use HEBO with learned transformations, whereas the guarantees concern the specified GP-UCB procedure. Practical acquisition choices and arm-selection hyperparameters are insufficiently documented, and the claimed public implementation is not linked within the PDF.
